one_liner: Cross-platform C event-loop library with built-in HTTP/WebSocket/MQTT; ~1.4-1.6x libevent/libuv echo throughput, ties libev/asio.
what_it_does: libhv is a reactor-style event loop (IO, timers, idle, signal and custom events) in C99, with TCP/UDP client/server/proxy, unpacking helpers, TLS, KCP, and HTTP/1.x/HTTP/2, WebSocket, MQTT and Redis modules on top. The C API is hloop_t/hio_t callbacks (hloop_create_tcp_server, hio_read, hio_write). An optional C++11 layer (EventLoop, EventLoopThreadPool, TcpServer, HttpServer, requests::get) follows muduo's one-loop-per-thread model. It is a separate API, not a drop-in for libevent or libuv.
how_it_is_fast: All connections on one loop share a single 8 KB per-loop read buffer, and hio_write calls send() directly, copying only the unsent remainder into a per-connection queue on EAGAIN; a steady-state echo therefore does no heap allocation per message. The benchmark's libuv server instead mallocs a read buffer and a write request per echo, and its libevent server allocates an evbuffer per read. The libev server uses a static buffer plus direct send(), which is why libev ties libhv. Supporting pieces: an fd-indexed io array, min-heap timers, and priority-ordered pending callbacks over epoll, kqueue, event ports, wepoll or select.
when_to_use: C or C++11 services that need one BSD-3 library for the event loop plus TCP/UDP, timers and HTTP/WebSocket/MQTT/Redis clients or servers, instead of stitching libuv or libevent to separate protocol libraries.
Many-connection request/response or proxy traffic with small messages (about 1 KB) where your current libuv/libevent code allocates per read or per write.
Code that must build on Linux, Windows, macOS, Android and iOS from one source tree (all five are built in CI) and cross-compile for ARM or MinGW.
C++ servers that want muduo-style one-loop-per-thread scaling through TcpServer::setThreadNum or EventLoopThreadPool with little code.
when_not_to_use: Existing libev or asio TCP code: in current CI libhv (115 MB/s) is level with libev and asio (both 118 MB/s), so porting buys no throughput.
You need to keep libevent or libuv call sites: there is no compatibility layer (issue #354 asked for one; only a partial sketch exists in comments), so every call site must be ported.
You want completion-based io_uring I/O: the io_uring backend (added 2026-03, off by default, needs liburing) only submits IORING_OP_POLL_ADD readiness polls and is not in any tagged release yet.

Untrusted input through the HTTP or DNS modules without your own review: three medium 2023 CVEs (CVE-2023-26146/26147/26148: XSS, response splitting, CRLF injection) are recorded for the HTTP layer, and an open report (#851, 2026-07) shows an ASan-confirmed heap overflow in protocol/dns.c (the WITH_PROTOCOL module, off by default).

Code that often starts, stops and destroys C++ TcpClient/UdpClient objects on a shared EventLoop from other threads: open issue #704 reports crashes on destruction and after repeated Stop/Start. Detailed docs are mostly Chinese (docs/cn).

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (both built by default via Makefile/configure, CMake or Bazel; also in vcpkg and xrepo)
integration.dependencies: none for the core; optional OpenSSL, GnuTLS or mbedTLS (TLS), nghttp2 (HTTP/2), liburing (io_uring backend), curl (deprecated), Lua, QuickJS, protobuf (hrpc)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 and C++11 (C++ layer optional via --without-evpp); GCC 4.8+ or MSVC 2015+; CMake 3.6+
integration.platforms: Linux (epoll, optional io_uring), Windows (wepoll over IOCP by default, else WSAPoll), macOS/BSD (kqueue), Solaris (event ports), Android, iOS; select fallback elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: One loop per thread. hio_write and hio_close are thread-safe (per-connection recursive mutex), and hloop_post_event is the thread-safe way to hand work to a loop. Other hio/timer calls are meant for the loop thread; the C++ layer offers runInLoop and isInLoopThread.

gotchas: The buffer passed to the read callback is the loop's shared read buffer. It is overwritten by the next read on any connection of that loop, so copy the data before storing or deferring it, or give the connection its own buffer with hio_set_readbuf.

Unsent data is copied into a per-connection write queue. Past 16 MB (max_write_bufsize default) hio_write closes the connection with ERR_OVER_LIMIT, so large senders need flow control through the write callback or hio_write_is_complete.
The hloop_post_event queue has no size limit (issue #818); the maintainer says to add your own cap if producers can outrun the loop.

hloop_new defaults to HLOOP_FLAG_AUTO_FREE, and the header forbids calling hloop_free on such a loop. For C++ TcpClient/UdpClient on an external loop, the maintainer advises heap allocation and deletion inside loop->runInLoop.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick libhv over uWebSockets when you need a general C event loop with TCP/UDP, timers and HTTP/WebSocket/MQTT/Redis clients on five platforms, not just a fast HTTP/WebSocket server. Pick it over PhotonLibOS (a C++ coroutine library whose catalogued win over asio is ~1.05x) when you want a plain C callback API; for io_uring-first designs, monoio (Rust) and the frevib echo server go further than libhv's poll-only io_uring backend.
verified_claims_summary: Setup: single-loop TCP echo servers on loopback, all written by the libhv author, driven by a libhv-based pingpong client sending 1 KB messages for 10 s. The README run (2021, 4 threads, 1000 connections, compiler and CPU not stated) measured libhv 215 MB/s vs libevent 157 and libuv 156 (~1.37x), with libev at 210. The 2026-09-25 GitHub Actions run I opened (ubuntu-24.04, gcc 13.3.0, distro libevent 2.1.12, libuv 1.48.0, libev 4.33, asio 1.28.1; 2 threads, 100 connections; CPU not logged) measured libhv 115 vs libevent 79 and libuv 77 (~1.46-1.49x), with libev and asio both at 118.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-25) under BSD-3-Clause, but the last tagged release is v1.3.4 (2025-10-25), so the io_uring backend and Redis client exist only on master; the library itself is easy to build and vendor.
